**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 14, verses 4–5:**

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿We did not send any Messenger except with the language of his people, so that he might make things clear for them. Then Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs: "Bring your people out of darknesses into the light, and remind them of the Days of Allah." Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾

This verse is a rebuttal and a critique of those who found it strange that Muhammad (ﷺ) should be sent. That is, O Muhammad, you are not an innovation among the Messengers. We sent you only to bring people out of darknesses into the light, following Our custom with Our Messengers, that We send them with the tongues of their nations, so that speech occurs with clear explanation and well-established expression. Then the differences among people who are not of the language would become dependent upon the people of the language, which is the language of the Prophet (upon him be blessings and peace). Allah made the reason for sending Messengers with the tongues of their peoples the seeking of clarity. Then (p-222) His saying "so that He leads astray" is a separate statement. That is, the Prophet (upon him be blessings and peace) only has the goal of conveying and making clear, and it is not within what he was charged with to guide or to lead astray. That is in the hand of Allah, who executes His preordained decree concerning it. For Him is the might that cannot be opposed and the wisdom that cannot be questioned for its reasons. There is no lord besides Him.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If a non-Arab objects by saying, "From where will this Messenger explain the Law to me when I do not understand him?", it is said to him: The people who know the language will translate for you, and that is sufficient for you. If he says, "From where will the miracle be made clear to me, and how will I understand the inimitability when I do not understand the language?", it is said to him: The proof against you is the submission of the people of eloquence, those who were thought to be capable of opposing it. By their submission the proof was established upon mankind, just as the proof was established in the miracle of Musa through the submission of the magicians, and in the miracle of 'Isa through the submission of the physicians.

The word "lisan" (tongue) in this verse is intended to mean language. Abu al-Sammal recited "bi-lisni qawmihi" (بِلِسْنِ قَوْمِهِ) with a sukoon on the sin and without an alif, like "rish" and "riyash" (feathers). We say that "lisn" and "lisan" in the sense of "language" are both used, but as for the organ (the tongue), it is not said "lisn" with a sukoon on the sin.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa…﴾, the verse. The signs of Allah are the staff, the hand, and the rest of the nine (signs). As for His saying: ﴿that bring your people out…﴾, its (grammatical) estimation is "bi-an" (by means of), i.e., "bi-an akhrij" (that you bring out). It is also permissible for "an" (أن) to be explanatory with no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection) for it. As for "the darknesses and the light," it is possible that they mean: from disbelief to faith. This is according to the apparent meaning of the command to the Children of Israel, in that before the sending of Musa, they were among themselves factions scattered in religion: a group together with the Copts in worshipping Pharaoh, and all of them upon nothing. This is the view of al-Tabari, which he related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. And if it is established that they were upon the religion of Ibrahim and Isra'il and the like, then the darknesses are humiliation and servitude, and the light is might through religion and prominence through the command of Allah, blessed and exalted.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of this verse, and of most verses concerning the mission of Musa (peace be upon him), is that it was directed to the Children of Israel specifically, regarding the Law for them, and commanding and forbidding them with the branches of the religion; and to Pharaoh and the nobles of his people, that they should reflect and take heed in the signs of Musa, so that they would acknowledge Allah, the Exalted, believe in Him, in Musa, and in his miracle, realize his prophethood, and send the Children of Israel with him.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not follow for them except by faith in him.

As for whether his mission to them was for the meaning of following him and entering into his law, this is not the apparent meaning of the story, and the unseen did not reveal that. Do you not see that Musa (peace be upon him) left them with the Children of Israel, and had they not followed him, he would have proceeded with his nation? And do you not see that he did not call the Copts as a whole, but rather he was conversing with those in authority? Also, his call to them was not in the manner of the call of Nuh, Hud, and Salih (peace be upon them) to their nations concerning their disbelief and sins, but rather in guidance and purification, and the sending of the Children of Israel. And what supports this is that if his call to Pharaoh and the Copts were according to the limits of his call to the Children of Israel, then why would he request, by the command of Allah, that they send the Children of Israel with him? Rather, he would request that all of them believe, follow his law, and the matter would be settled. Also, if he had been sent to the Copts, Allah would have returned him to them when Pharaoh and his soldiers drowned, but they were not his nation, so he was not returned to them.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Those who hold that Musa (peace be upon him) was sent to all of them argue with the Exalted's saying in more than one verse: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [7:103], and ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [27:12]. And Allah knows best.

(p-224) As for His saying: ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾, the verse. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded Musa to admonish his people by warning them of the vengeances of Allah that He sent upon the disbelieving nations before them, and by enumerating His blessings upon them in the earlier occasions, and upon others among the people of His obedience, so that their conduct would follow the path of those upon whom He bestowed favor, and that they would flee from the path of those upon whom the vengeances descended. He expressed the blessings and the vengeances by "days" because they occur within days. In this expression is the magnification of these events that are being reminded of. From this meaning is their saying: "a grievous day," "a frowning day," and "a cheerful day." The literal meaning is the description of what occurred in it of hardship or joy. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: the Days of Allah are His blessings, and from another group that they said: the Days of Allah are His vengeances.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The word "days" encompasses both meanings, because the reminder occurs by both aspects together.

As for His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿for every steadfast, grateful person﴾, He only intended: for every believer who reflects upon himself. He took from the attributes of the believer two qualities that combine most of the virtues and encompass the most excellent of deeds.

There, "sū' al-'adhāb" (the worst torment) was explained as being slaughter and sparing of women; here, by "sū' al-'adhāb" it indicates types other than slaughter and sparing, and slaughter and sparing are coordinated after it. The word "al-balā'" (trial) in this verse may mean hardship (miḥnah), and it may mean testing (ikhtibār); the meaning is close.

"Ta'adhdhana" (تأذّن) means "adhdhana," i.e., he informed, similar to "akrama" and "takarrama," and "awʿada" and "tawaʿʿada." This announcement from Him is linked to an execution and decree that had preceded it. What is in this form "tafaʿʿala" of striving and beginning, when attributed to humans, is negated with respect to Allah, the Exalted. As for the Arabs' saying "ta'allama" in the sense of "a'lama" (to inform), its past form is rejected according to what Ya'qub mentioned, like the poet's saying:

"Learn — may you not be disgraced by curses..." (verse incomplete)

and similar.

Some scholars said: the increase beyond gratitude is not in this world; rather it is from the blessings of the Hereafter, and this world is less than that.

and the distance of my family and the harshness of my kin, she would have bitten the tips of her hand from longing."

Talhah ibn Musarraf recited: "mimmā tad'ūnanā" with a single, doubled nun.

and similar.

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God, Originator of the heavens and the earth? He invites you that He may forgive you some of your sins and grant you respite until a specified term." They said: "You are only mortals like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾ ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only mortals like you, but God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. It is not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave. And upon God let the believers rely."﴾ ﴿And why should we not rely upon God, when He has guided us to our paths? We will surely bear patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us. And upon God let those who rely [upon Him] rely.﴾

His saying: ﴿Ara fi Allah [Is there doubt about God]﴾ has an implied pronoun in it. Its estimated form, according to many grammarians, is: "Is there doubt about His divinity (ilahiyyah)?" Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Is there doubt about His oneness (wahdaniyyah)?"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Some people claimed that Abu 'Ali only resorted to this expression to safeguard the Mu'tazila position, and to remove what the word "divinity" (ilahiyyah) may imply among attributes according to its generality; the word "oneness" (wahdaniyyah) frees one from that possibility.

"Fatir" means the one who originates and initiates. Mentioning this attribute is an argument against those who doubt, meaning: doubt about one whose attribute is this. He mentioned the attribute, which is in the accusative case, to remove doubt. As for His saying: ﴿min dhunubikum [some of your sins]﴾, some grammarians held that "min" here is superfluous (za'idah). Sibawayh refuses that it be superfluous and considers it to indicate partiality (li-al-tab'id), which is a sound meaning. This is because the promise was made concerning the forgiveness of polytheism and what accompanies it of sins, while the sins that one of them commits after his faith remain unmentioned, so that they remain under God's will, Exalted is He. Forgiveness is thus promised only for a part, and so the meaning of "min" is correct.

(p-230) As for His saying: ﴿wa-yu'akhkhirakum ila ajalin musamma [and grant you respite until a specified term]﴾, the discussion of it has already preceded in surah al-A'raf, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-li-kulli ummatin ajal [For every nation there is a term]﴾ [al-A'raf: 34], and I brought it there because of the apparent contradiction between the two verses. It is fitting here to mention the issue of the one who is killed: is his term cut short, or is that his fixed term decreed for him? The first is the view of the Mu'tazila, and the second is the view of the People of the Sunna. The Mu'tazila say: "If he had not killed him, he would have lived; and this is the cause of retaliation (qawad)." A group of the People of the Sunna said: "If he had not killed him, he would have died a natural death." Abu al-Ma'ali said: "All of this is confusion (takhabbut). Rather, it is his term which preceded in the divine decree that he would die in that state, so it is impossible for anything else to occur. If we suppose that had he not killed him [the victim would have lived], and we suppose along with that that God's knowledge had preceded that he would not kill him, then his case remains within the realm of possibility, whether he lives or is killed, whatever God's knowledge precedes concerning it."

The saying of the disbelievers: ﴿in antum illa basharun mithlunaa [You are only mortals like us]﴾ contains a denial of the possibility of sending a human messenger. Some people said: rather, they intended to deem it impossible, and they followed the path of the Brahmins or those philosophers who say that species do not admit this kind of difference.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of their speech does not require that they overlooked this matter so completely. What supports what I have mentioned is that they asked them to bring a sign and a clear authority. Had their sending been impossible in their view, they would not have asked them for proof. It is also possible that their demand for authority from them was made by way of challenge, meaning: your sending is impossible, otherwise bring a clear authority, that is, you will never do that. This possibility strengthens the view of those who incline toward the doctrine of the philosophers.

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only mortals like you,"﴾ the meaning: you spoke truly in your saying "we are human" in terms of persons and creation, but we differ by God's grace and bounty, which He bestows upon whom He wills, so they differed from them in meaning (bi-al-ma'na), unlike His saying: ﴿as if they were startled donkeys [al-Muddaththir: 50]﴾, for that concerns meaning, not appearance.

His saying: ﴿wa-ma kana lana an na'tiyakum bi-sultanin illa bi-idhni Allah [It is not for us to bring you an authority except by God's leave]﴾: when a person says this of himself, or it is said to him concerning something within his power, its meaning is prohibition and restriction; if it concerns something beyond his power, its meaning is the total negation of that matter. This verse is similar. Al-Mahdawi said: its wording is that of a prohibition, but its meaning is negation. The lam in His saying "fa-l-yatawakkal" is the lam of command. The majority read it with sukun, while al-Hasan read it with kasra. Vocalizing it with kasra is its original form, and making it sukun is a request for lightness, due to its frequent use, and to distinguish it from the lam of kay, whose vowel is obligatory by consensus.

His saying: ﴿wa-ma lana alla natawakkala 'ala Allah [And why should we not rely upon God]﴾ to the end of the verse: the messengers posed it to them in the manner of rebuke, regarding the pretext for not relying upon God, when He has bestowed favour upon them, guided them to the path of salvation, and preferred them over His creation. Then they swore that they would surely bear patiently the harm inflicted upon them for the sake of God, Exalted is He. The "ma" in His saying ﴿ma adhaytumuna [whatever harm you inflict upon us]﴾ is verbal (masdariyyah). According to Sibawayh, when it stands alone it is a particle, but with the verbal noun that follows it, it forms a noun. Some grammarians said that the verbal "ma" standing alone is a noun. It is possible that "ma" in this place means "alladhi" (that which), so that in "adhaytumuna" there is a returning pronoun whose estimated form is "adhaytumuunahu," and it may not be attached to it because the preposition is elided; this is the view of Sibawayh, while al-Akhfash permits it.

It was also said: it means one who compels people to what they dislike.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is what is understood from the word. Qatada and others explained "al-jabbar" as the one who refuses to say "There is no god but God." "Al-'anid" is the one who is obstinate and does not submit.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 14, verses 18–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿The likeness of those who disbelieved in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day. They have no power over anything of what they have earned. That is the far-reaching error.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered that Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth? If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾

There is disagreement concerning what raises "mathal" (likeness, similitude). The position of Sibawayh is that the implied construction is: "in what is recited to you," or "the likeness of those who disbelieved is related." The position of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' is that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is "like ashes," and the implied meaning for them is: "The likeness of those who disbelieved is like ashes." It has also been related from al-Farra' that he holds that "mathal" is superfluous (mulgha), and that the meaning is: "Those who disbelieved, their deeds are like ashes." It has been said that it is a subject, and "their deeds" is a second subject, "like ashes" is the predicate of the second, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first. This, in my view, is the most preferred of the opinions. It is as if you had said: "What is gathered in the soul concerning those who disbelieved is this clause mentioned, namely: their deeds are like ashes." This principle, in my view, applies to the implied construction in His exalted saying: "the likeness of Paradise." The deeds and efforts of the disbelievers, in their corruption at the time of need and their vanishing, are likened to ashes which the wind scatters and disperses by its strength, so that no trace remains and nothing from it is gathered. He described the day as "stormy," though stormy is really an attribute of the wind, because the wind occurs during that day. From this same meaning is the saying of the poet:

"You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, during the night journey, and you slept, while the night of the riding camels does not sleep."

And from it is the saying of another:

"Two days cloudy, and a day sunny."

So the deeds of the disbelievers, because of their vanishing, give them no power over anything from them. Nafi' alone, and Abu Ja'far, read "al-riyah" (the winds), while the rest read "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular. This has been mentioned previously and its meaning fully discussed, praise be to Allah.

His saying "that" (dhalika) refers to their being in this state, and to a condition like this one of uncertainty. "al-Dalal al-Ba'id" (the far-reaching error): that in which its follower has gone deep and strayed far from the clear path of salvation. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Ibn Abi Bakr read "fi yawmin 'asif" with the noun "yawm" put in the genitive construction with "'asif," and this is clear.

al-Sulami read "alam tar" with a sukun on the ra', meaning "alam ta'lam" (have you not known), from the sight of the heart. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "khalaqa al-samawat" (He created the heavens), while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "khaliq al-samawat" (Creator of the heavens). The reasoning of the first is that it is a past verb, so it is mentioned as such; the reasoning of the second is that it is like "Fatir al-samawat wa al-ard" [Ibrahim: 10] and "Faliq al-isbah" [al-An'am: 96]. His saying "bil-haqq" (in truth) means: by what is due to exist in terms of the interests of His servants and the execution of His prior decree, and so that it may indicate Him and His power. Then, Blessed and Exalted is He, threatened with His saying: "If He wills, He can take you away" (in-yasha' yudhhibkum), meaning: He would annihilate you and efface your traces. His saying "bi-khalqin jadid" (with a new creation) may be taken to mean: from the remnants of the children of Adam, and it may have other meanings. His saying "wa ma dhalika 'ala Allah bi-'aziz" means: it is not impossible.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 14, verse 21:**

The Exalted said:

﴿And they will all come forth before God, and the weak will say to those who were arrogant: "Indeed, we were your followers, so can you avail us anything against the punishment of God?" They will say: "Had God guided us, we would have guided you. It is all the same for us whether we lament or endure patiently; for us there is no escape."﴾

His saying, "﴿And they came forth to God all together﴾": its meaning is that they came out into the open (*al-bāraz*), which is the wide, open ground, like *al-barāḥ*, *al-arāʾ* and *al-khabār*. This term is used metaphorically for the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. His saying "*tabaʿan*" (followers) may be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), in which case it is like their saying "a day of justice" (*yawmu ʿadlin*) and "a day of war" (*yawmu ḥarbin*). It may also be the plural of *tābiʿ* (follower), on the pattern of *gāʾib* and *gaybun* (absent), and this is the interpretation of al-Ṭabarī.

People have explained "*al-ḍuʿafāʾ*" (the weak) as the followers, and "*al-mustakbirīn*" (the arrogant) as the leaders and men of opinion. Their saying "*mughnūna ʿannā*" (can you avail us) is from *al-ghanāʾ* (benefit), which is the benefit one person gives another in defence or otherwise.

The alif in His saying "*ajaziʿnā*" (whether we lament) is the alif of equalization (*alif al-taswiya*), not the interrogative alif. It is like His saying "*am lam tundhir-hum*" (whether you warn them or do not warn them). *Al-maḥīṣ* (escape) means refuge and shelter; it is derived from *ḥāṣa yaḥīṣu*, meaning to flee and run away. From this usage is the saying in the hadith of Heraclius (Hiraql): "*fa-ḥāṣū ḥaysata ḥumuri al-waḥshi ilā al-abwāb*" (they fled in a rush like wild donkeys to the gates).

It is also narrated from Ibn Zayd and from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb that the people of the Fire say: "Those of the People of Paradise attained mercy only through patience in obedience to God, so let us be patient." They are patient for five hundred years, and it benefits them nothing. Then they say: "Let us lament," and they wail, shriek and weep for another five hundred years, and it benefits them nothing. Then they say this statement that is in the verse. The apparent meaning of the verse is that they say it at the station of presentation, at the time of coming forth before God, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 14, verses 22–23:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And Satan will say, when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. And I had no authority over you, except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieve in your association of me with Allah before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers there is a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever by the permission of their Lord. Their greeting therein will be: "Peace."﴾

What is meant here by "al-Shaytan" is Iblis al-Aqdam (the Ancient Iblis) himself. It has been related in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), through the route of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection two preachers will stand: one of them is Iblis, who will stand among the disbelievers with these words, and the second is 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him), who will stand with his saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me, [saying], "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]." Some scholars said: Iblis will stand as the evil preacher, speaking truthfully by this verse.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

According to the meaning of these narrations, the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ is: a group has been determined for entry into the Fire and a group for entry into the Garden, and all of that is at the place of standing (al-mawqif).

It has been related in a hadith that Iblis only stands with these words in the Fire, over its people, when they say: ﴿Is there for us any way of escape?﴾ [Ibrahim: 21], in the preceding verse.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

According to this narration, the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the matter has been decided﴾ is: the people of the Fire have been placed in the Fire, and the people of the Garden (in the Garden). This is the interpretation of al-Tabari. "Qudiya" (it has been decided) may be used in matters to express an action, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the matter was decided, and it settled upon al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44], and it may be used to express a determination to do something, as in His saying: ﴿The matter about which you both inquire has been decided﴾ [Yusuf: 41].

"Al-wa'd" (the promise) in this verse is in its usual sense regarding good: that is, Allah promised them bliss if they believed, and Iblis promised them victory and hope if they disbelieved. It is known that Allah's promise is coupled with His warning, and it happened that they did not follow the pursuit of Allah's promise, so they fell into His warning. From this it came that it is as if Iblis broke his promise to them.

Al-sultan (authority) means clear proof. His saying: ﴿except that I called you﴾ is an exceptive clause of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and "an" (that) is in the accusative position. It may also be in the nominative position, in the sense: "except that the one who substitutes for authority (is) my calling you," so this is in meaning like the saying of the poet:

...................

؎ Their greeting among them is a painful striking

The meaning of His saying: ﴿and you responded to me﴾ is: you saw with your insight what I called you to, and you believed it to be the opinion, and your reflection leaned toward it.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Some people mentioned that in this place taqlid (blind imitation) is nullified. In this claim there is weakness, if it is taken that way, and taqlid, although it is invalid, its corruption is from other than this place.

It may be intended by authority in this verse: dominance, power and sovereignty, that is: I did not compel you nor frighten you with a strength from me, but I presented to you something and your opinion inclined toward it.

His saying: ﴿so do not blame me﴾ he means by his claim: since there is no sin on me, ﴿but blame yourselves﴾ for your bad judgment and your lack of firmness, for you only came to follow me out of your own insight and acquisition.

"Al-muṣrikh" means the one who gives aid, and "al-ṣārikh" means the one who seeks aid. From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ We, when a frightened crier came to us... the crying was for him a cutting of the tendons

It is said: "ṣarakha al-rajul wa-aṣraka ghayrahu" (the man cried out and caused another to cry out). As for "al-ṣarīkh," it is a verbal noun on the pattern of "al-barīḥ," and it is described by it, as one says "rajul 'adl" (a just man) and the like.

Ḥamzah, al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "bi-muṣrikhiyy" with a kasra on the yā' (ya'), likening it to the yā' of the pronoun in His saying "bi-muṣrikhiyyihi." Al-Zajjaj rejected this reading and said: it is poor and reprehensible. Al-Qasim ibn Ma'n said of it that it is correct, and Abu 'Ali justified it. Abu Hatim related that Abu 'Amr considered it good, and Abu Hatim denied this against Abu 'Amr.

Regarding these opinions, the objection is that all of these are from the herbs (najm), not from trees, and Allah only gave the example of a tree, so these are not called trees except by metaphor. The Almighty's saying:

﴿Say to My servants who have believed: let them establish the prayer and spend secretly and openly from what We have provided them, before there comes a Day in which there is no trading and no friendship.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. He subjected to you the ships to run upon the sea by His command, and He subjected to you the rivers.﴾ ﴿And He subjected to you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses, and He subjected to you the night and the day.﴾ ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him. And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is a great wrongdoer and ungrateful.﴾

"Al-'ibad" is the plural of "'abd" (servant). Its customary usage is one of honour, in contrast to "al-'abid" (slaves).

As for His saying ﴿let them establish the prayer﴾ [yuqimu], a group of grammarians said that its jussive ending (jazm) is due to the elision of the imperative lam (lam al-amr), following the line of the poet:

Muhammad, let your soul be ransomed; every soul [is ransom for you].

Sibawayh transmitted this line, but he said that this usage is permissible only in poetry. Another group, including Abu 'Ali and others, said that it is a present-tense verb in the jussive because it has the meaning of the imperative verb, since the intended meaning is "establish" (aqimu). This is like the way a declinable noun is made indeclinable in the vocative in your saying "Ya Zayd," when it is likened to "qabla" and "ba'da." Sibawayh also said that it is the response of an implied conditional clause contained in the beginning of the verse, its estimated form being: "If you say to them, 'Establish,' they will establish."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the response of the command, whose meaning is indicated by His saying "Say," is this: the word "say" in this verse is taken to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shariah," [so that the sense is] "they will establish the prayer." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down water from the sky, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you, and subjected to you the ships to run upon the sea by His command, and subjected to you the rivers﴾ and so on, is a reminder of Allah's blessings and an alert to His power, which contains kindness to mankind, so that the proof is established in two ways. "Allah" is the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhi" is its predicate (khabar). Whoever is informed of this statement and it becomes firmly established in his soul, believes, prays, and spends. His saying ﴿of the fruits﴾ may be understood with "min" as partitive, so that the meaning is some of the produce of the trees, and what is poisonous or harmful is excluded. It may also be that "min" is explanatory of the genus, as if He said: "brought forth thereby provision for you consisting of fruits." Some people said that "min" is superfluous here, but this is not permissible according to Sibawayh, because it occurs in a positive statement, while it is permissible according to al-Akhfash. "Al-fulk" is the plural of "fulk" (ship), and its discussion has been mentioned several times before.

His saying "by His command" is a verbal noun from "amara, ya'muru" (to command). This refers to the speech subsisting in His essence, like Allah's saying to the seas, the earth, and all other things at the moment of bringing them into existence: "Be!" Its meaning is: "Be in such a state, and in such a manner." In this is a gradual process: the rotation of the ship includes the subjection of the sea and the subjection of the winds. As for the subjection of the rivers, it is their gushing forth in every land and their being made to yield for irrigation and all other benefits.

"Da'ibayn" means "continuing without cease." From this is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the owner of the camel that wept and came to him in distress: "This camel complained to me that you starve it and overwork it." Al-Tabari related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, traced back (yarfa'uhu) to Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: its meaning is: constant in obedience to Allah. If it is meant that it is intended obedience like the obedience of human servants, then this is far-fetched. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾ is directed to the human species as a whole. That is, mankind collectively has been given of everything that is suitable to be asked for and benefited from. This does not apply uniformly to each individual person. Rather, these blessings are distributed among mankind, and so it is said, in accordance with this, to all of them: "You have been given such-and-such," by way of enumerating the blessing. It has also been said that the meaning is: "And He gave you of all that you would have asked of Him, had you asked."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is close to the first explanation. The "ma" in His saying, glorified be He, ﴿ما سألتموه﴾ (what you asked of Him) may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle, and the pronoun in "sa'altumuhu" then refers to Allah, blessed and exalted be He. It may also be that "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and the pronoun refers to "alladhi." Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim and Ibn 'Abbas read ﴿من كلٍّ ما سألتموه﴾ with tanwin on "kull" (kullin). This is also the reading of al-Hasan, Qatada, and Salam, and it has been transmitted from Nafi'. The meaning is: "And He gave you, from all these created things mentioned before, that which is suitable to be asked for the purpose of benefit from it." Thus "ma" in His saying ﴿ما سألتموه﴾ is the second object of "ataakum" (gave you). Some people said that in this reading "ma" is a negation, meaning: "He gave you something of every kind, which you did not ask for," and the second object is our statement "shay'an" (something). By this, He enumerated the blessing in His preference of them through what mankind had not asked for of the blessings, and what they had asked for had not come to mind.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the explanation of al-Dahhak. As for the first reading, with the idafa of "kull" to "ma," it is necessary to supply the second object as "a part" or "something" or something similar.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [An-Nahl: 18], that is, because of its abundance and greatness, in the senses and faculties, and in bringing into existence from non-existence, and in guidance to faith and other things. Talq ibn Habib said: "The right of Allah is too heavy for the servants to fulfil, and His blessings are too numerous for the servants to count. So be turning to Him in repentance in the morning, and be turning to Him in repentance in the evening." Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever sees Allah's blessing upon him only in his food and his drink has little knowledge and his punishment is near."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind﴾ means by it the species and the genus. The meaning is: these qualities exist in him, namely wrongdoing and disbelief. If these qualities come from one who denies, then they are of one description, and if they come from one who is disobedient, then they are of another description.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 14, verses 35–37:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols."﴾ ﴿"My Lord, they have led many people astray. Whoever follows me, he is of me; and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, that they may be grateful."﴾

The meaning: "Remember when Abraham said." "The city" (al-balad) is Makkah. "Secure" (aminan) means that there is security in it, so it is described as secure figuratively, as in His saying: ﴿on a stormy day﴾ (Ibrahim: 18), and as the poet said:

"And the night of the riding camels does not sleep."

"Keep me far" (ijnubni) means "prevent me," as one says: janabahu kadha, janabbahu, and ajnabahu, meaning he prevented him from the matter and kept him away from it. Al-Jahdari and al-Thaqafi read "wa-ajnibni" with a hamza and a kasra on the nun. "My sons" (baniyya) refers to his biological descendants, and for this reason his supplication was answered regarding them, whereas the rest of his offspring worshipped idols. This supplication from the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be prayer and peace, implies extreme fear for himself and for those in his rank. How, then, would he fear worshipping an idol? Yet this verse should be taken as an example in fearing (God) and in seeking a good end.

"Idols" (al-asnam) are those carved in the likeness of human beings; what is carved in a form other than human is called awthan (idols or images). This was stated by al-Tabari, on the authority of Mujahid. He attributed to the idols that they "led many people astray" figuratively, since they were the object of misguidance and the means set up for error, and deeds arise from them. The true act of misguidance belongs only to the one who invented it.

His saying: ﴿whoever disobeys me﴾ apparently refers to disbelief, in parallel with His saying: ﴿whoever follows me, he is of me﴾. If that is the case, then His saying ﴿indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ means: by Your turning (in mercy) toward the disbelievers until they believe, not that he meant God forgives a disbeliever. Rather, what led him to this expression was the good speech, the fine utterance, and the beautiful manners that he imposed upon himself, (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Qatadah said: "Listen to the words of the Friend. By God, they were neither slanderers nor cursers." Likewise the prophet of God, Jesus, upon him be peace, said: ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 118). Al-Tabari also cited, by isnad, a hadith from Abd Allah ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited these two verses and then supplicated for his community, and he was given good news concerning them. Ibrahim al-Taymi used to say: "Who can feel safe for himself after the Friend's fear for himself of worshipping idols?"

His saying: ﴿from my offspring﴾ means Isma'il, upon him be peace. The background is that when Sarah became jealous of Hajar after she had borne Isma'il, Abraham, upon him be peace, was distressed by the two of them. He rode the Buraq, along with Hajar and the infant, and in a single day he came from al-Sham to the floor of Makkah. He dismounted and left his son and his maidservant there, then rode away on the same day. All of this was by revelation from God, blessed and exalted. When he turned away, he supplicated with the content of this verse. As for how Hajar remained, what she did, and the rest of the account of Isma'il, these are in al-Bukhari's book, in the biographies (al-siyar), and elsewhere. The "min" in His saying ﴿from my offspring﴾ is partitive, because Ishaq was in al-Sham.

"The valley" (al-wadi) is what lies between two mountains, and it is not a condition that it contain water. This verse implies that Abraham, upon him be peace, knew from God, exalted be He, that He would not waste Hajar and her son in that valley, and that He would provide them with water. He only looked at the distant outcome when he said ﴿without cultivation﴾. Had he not known this from God, he would have said "without water," given the condition of the valley at that time.

His saying ﴿by Your Sacred House﴾: either the House had existed long before, as is narrated, before the Flood, and its knowledge was with Abraham; or he said it when God, exalted be He, had informed him that he would build there a house for God, which would be sacred. The meaning: sacred against the tyrants, and that its sanctity should not be violated or its right held in contempt. This was stated by Qatadah and others. His using the pronoun plural in His saying "that they may establish" shows that God had informed him that this child would have descendants there and would have offspring. The lam in His saying "that they may establish" is the lam of purpose (kay), and this is its apparent meaning, with it being connected to "I have settled." The address (al-nida') is a parenthetical interjection. It is also permissible for it to be the lam of command, as if he were asking God to grant them success in establishing prayer, and then he set forth a phrase obligating them to establish prayer. In the wording, according to this interpretation, there is some figurative usage, which the meaning connects and makes right.

"Hearts" (al-af'idah) means the hearts, plural of fu'ad. It was named so because of its being fa'ada (pierced/burned through), derived from f-'-d, and from it comes al-muf'tad, which is the place where a fire is kindled to roast meat. Ibn 'Amir, according to one variant transmitted from him, read "fa-aj'al afyidah" with a ya after the hamza. His saying ﴿from among people﴾ is partitive, and its intended meaning is the believers. Mujahid said: "If Abraham had said 'the hearts of people,' Persians and Romans would have crowded upon the House." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The Jews and Christians would have performed Hajj to it."

"Tahwi" (incline) means to travel with haste and determined purpose. From it is the poet's saying:

"When you hurl it toward the mountain passes, you see it plunging through their ravines like the plunge of a falcon."

And from it is the transmitted verse:

"Heading toward Makkah, seeking guidance, the believers among the jinn are not like their kinds."

Salamah ibn Abd Allah read "tuhwi" with a damma on the ta', from ahwa, which is the aforementioned verb transitive by the hamza. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad ibn Ali, and Mujahid read "tahwi" with a fatha on the ta' and the waw. This verb, which derives from hawa, is transitive with "ila" when it is connected with travel and purpose.

It is narrated from Muslim ibn Muhammad al-Ta'ifi that when he, upon him be peace, supplicated that the inhabitants of Makkah be provided with fruits, God sent Jibril, upon him be peace, who uprooted with his wing a piece of land from Palestine, and it is said from al-Urdunn. He brought it and circumambulated the House with it seven times, and placed it near Makkah. This is al-Ta'if, and it was named after this story. It is the place of the Thaqif, and it has trees and fruits.

(p-257) Ibrahim's aim, peace be upon him, was to draw attention to the brevity of his supplication and to his entrusting the matter to what Allah knows of his desires, his eagerness for the guidance of his sons, his gentleness toward them, and other things besides. Then he turned to praising Allah, the Exalted, as the Knower of the unseen, and to thanking Him for His gifts. These verses are among those that show that Allah's knowledge of things is complete and detailed.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare fixedly.﴾ ﴿Hastening forward, with heads raised, their glance does not return to them, and their hearts are void.﴾ ﴿And warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, respite us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Did you not swear before that you would have no cessation?﴾

This verse, in its entirety, contains a warning to the wrongdoers and consolation to the wronged. The address in His saying "do not think" is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the prohibition is intended for someone other than him, one who would fittingly suppose such a thing. Talha ibn Musarrif read "wa-la tahsibi Allaha ghafilan" with the nun dropped, and likewise "fa-la tahsibi Allaha mukhlifa wa'dihi." Abu Haywa, 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "nu'akhkhiruhum" with the nun of majesty, while the majority read "yu'akhkhiruhum" with the ya', meaning Allah the Exalted. "Tashkhasu" means: they will fix their gaze in terror, and because of the extremity of that, it resembles the staring of one at the point of death.

"Al-muhti'" (the one who hastens): the one who hurries in his walk, as said by Ibn Jubayr and Qatada, and this is in humiliation and abjectness, like the hurrying of a captive who is afraid, and the like. This is the most preferred of the opinions. Camels may be described as "ihta'" in the sense of hastening, and their hastening is rarely except out of fear of the whip or the like. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And with a hastening, lean-sided [mount], as if its reins
were at the top of a trunk of a tall, pruned palm."

And from this is the saying of 'Imran ibn Hattan:

"When a summoning caller calls us, we hasten to his call,
a hearing caller, and they drove us and herded us."

And from it is the saying of Ibn Mufarragh:

"In Dijla is their dwelling, and indeed I have seen them
in Dijla hastening toward the hearing."

And from this is the saying of another:

"With a hastening, obedient [mount], as if its halter
at the front of a wild tree from a tree-lined thicket is restrained."

Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Duha said: "Ihta'" is intense staring without blinking. Ibn Zayd said: it is the one who does not raise his head. Abu 'Ubayda said: "Ihta'" may apply to both meanings together: hastening and continuous gazing.

"Al-muqni'" is the one who raises his head forward with his face toward something. From this is the saying of the poet:

"They come early to the thorn trees with raised heads,
their molars like the sharp-beaked hawks."

(p-260) He describes camels as "iqna'" while grazing on the tops of trees. Al-Hasan said, in explaining this verse: the faces of people on the Day of Resurrection will be turned toward the sky, and no one will look at anyone. Al-Mubarrad mentioned, as is related, that "iqna'" is found in Arabic speech with the meaning of lowering the head out of humiliation, but the first is more well-known.

His saying: ﴿their glance does not return to them﴾ means: they do not blink out of dread, anguish, and the severity of the situation.

His saying: ﴿and their hearts are void﴾ is a pure simile, since they are not literally air. The aspect of comparison may be the emptiness of the hearts from good, hope, and expectation of mercy, so they are broken open, resembling air in its being emptied of things and its being pierced through. It may also be the agitation of their hearts and their surging in their chests, and that they come and go and reach, as has been narrated, their throats; in that they are like air, which is always in agitation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On these two aspects the heart of the coward and the heart of a man agitated in his affairs are likened to air. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And do not be among the companions of every weak-hearted one, air,
hollow within, whose ribs are broken, like the young camel's..."

From this is the saying of Hassan:

"Unless you convey to Abu Sufyan from me:
you are hollow, empty, and air."

"As if the saddle upon it, above a mountain-like lone one
of the crane-like birds, its breast is air."

The meaning is that it is in the utmost lightness in its fleeing.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And warn the people﴾ and the verse. The day is intended as the Day of Resurrection, and it is in the accusative as an object of "warn." It is not permissible for it to be an adverbial of time, because the Resurrection is not a place for warning. His saying "fa-yaqulu" is in the nominative as a conjunction with His saying "ya'tihim." His saying ﴿Did you not﴾ to the end of the verse means: it will be said to them, and this is omitted for brevity, since the meaning indicates it. His saying ﴿what you have of cessation﴾ is the thing sworn to, conveying the meaning. And ﴿min zawal﴾ means: from the earth after death, that is, no resurrection from the graves. (p-٢٦٦) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And you will see the criminals that Day bound together in shackles.﴾ ﴿Their garments will be of pitch, and fire will cover their faces.﴾ ﴿That Allah may recompense every soul for what it earned. Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿This is a notification for mankind, that they may be warned by it, and that they may know that He is but one God, and that those of understanding may take heed.﴾

"Al-mujrimun" (the criminals) are the disbelievers. "Muqarranin" means bound in a "qarn," which is the rope with which the heads of camels and cattle are tied. From this is the poet's saying:

"And the son of a she-camel that is not yet fully grown, when he is tied with a rope, cannot withstand the charge of the full-grown, strong camels."

"Al-asfad" means the shackles; its singular is "safad." It is said: "safadahu," "asfadahu," and "saffadahu" when he shackled him. The verbal noun is "al-sifad." From this is the saying of Salama ibn Jandal:

"And Zayd al-Khayl has met with shackling, biting on forearm and on shin-bone."

The same word is used for giving. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"So I did not offer you, may you not be cursed, anything of gifts."

(p-٢٦٧) "Al-sarabil" means shirts. "Al-qatiran" is that with which camels are coated with tar for scabies, and fire has an intense blaze in it. For this reason Allah made the shirts of the people of the Fire from it. It is also read with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the ta', with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', and with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the ta'. 'Umar, 'Ali, al-Hasan (with a variant), Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, 'Alqama, Sinan ibn Salama, 'Ikrima, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Jubayr, al-Kalbi, Qatada, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it as "qatrin ani." "Al-qatr" is tin, and it is said to be copper. It is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It is not tar, but copper, with which they are clothed." "Ani" is an adjective, meaning that which is molten and hot, whose heat has reached its extreme. Al-Hasan said: "Hell has been kindled over it since it was created, so its heat has reached its extreme."

The majority of reciters read "wujuhahum" with a fatha, and "al-naru" with a damma. Ibn Mas'ud read it the reverse. The first is like the verse: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1], where covering is literal. The second is like the saying of the poet:

"They are covered over until their dogs do not bark, and they do not ask about the dark one approaching."

Here the covering is used figuratively, as if the faces' arrival at the Fire were a covering.

The lam is connected to a hidden verb, whose estimate is: "I execute this punishment upon the criminals so that in it there may be the recompense of the evildoer for his evil." The word "kasb" (earning) is used in a way that includes both the evildoer and the doer of good, to draw attention to the fact that the doer of good is also recompensed with good for his goodness.

There is no god but Him. It was said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "How does Allah call the servants to account at one time with their great number?" He said: "As He provides for them at one time."

Yahya ibn 'Imara and Ahmad ibn Yazid ibn Usayd read "wa-liyandharu" with a fatha on the ya' and the dhal. The Arabs say: "Nadhartu bi-kadha" when I become aware of it, guard against it, and prepare for it.

The same word is used for giving. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"So I did not offer you, may you not be cursed, anything of gifts."

"Al-qatr" is tin, and it is said to be copper. It is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It is not tar, but copper, with which they are clothed." "Ani" is an adjective, meaning that which is molten and hot, whose heat has reached its extreme. Al-Hasan said: "Hell has been kindled over it since it was created, so its heat has reached its extreme."

Here the covering is used figuratively, as if the faces' arrival at the Fire were a covering.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿That Allah may recompense﴾: that is, so that Allah may recompense. The lam is connected to a hidden verb, whose estimate is: "I execute this punishment upon the criminals so that in it there may be the recompense of the evildoer for his evil." The word "kasb" (earning) is used in a way that includes both the evildoer and the doer of good, to draw attention to the fact that the doer of good is also recompensed with good for his goodness.

There is no god but Him. It was said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "How does Allah call the servants to account at one time with their great number?" He said: "As He provides for them at one time."

His saying: ﴿This is a notification for mankind﴾, the verse refers to the Qur'an and the warning it contains. He described it with the verbal noun in His saying "balagh" (notification), and the meaning is: "This is a thing that is a notification for mankind, and it is so that they may be warned by it." The majority read "wa-liyundharu" with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the dhal, in the passive form of the verb. Yahya ibn 'Imara and Ahmad ibn Yazid ibn Usayd read "wa-liyandharu" with a fatha on the ya' and the dhal. The Arabs say: "Nadhartu bi-kadha" when I become aware of it, guard against it, and prepare for it.

It is narrated that His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿and that those of understanding may take heed﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.
